title: FTP vs CP vs MLSS
goal: Explain what FTP, CP and MLSS each measure, the evidence that they differ, and both sides of the CP–MLSS debate.

steps.title: Three numbers, three definitions
steps.text:
Three numbers are often treated as one, but each is found a different way:

| | what it is | how it's found |
|---|---|---|
| [FTP](g:ftp) | power for about an hour | usually 95% of a 20-min all-out effort |
| CP | where the power–duration curve levels off | 3–5 efforts of 2–15 min |
| [MLSS](g:mlss) | top power with steady [lactate](g:lactate) | 4–5 rides of 30 min on different days; lactate may rise no more than 1 mmol·L⁻¹ from min 10 to 30 |

[[c:ftp-def]] [[c:mlss-def]]

FTP is a performance number. CP and MLSS are each meant to mark the [maximal metabolic steady state](g:maximal-metabolic-steady-state), the top of the [heavy domain](g:heavy-domain).

claims.text: FTP is defined as the power a cyclist can hold in a quasi-steady state for about 60 min, and is usually taken as 95% of a 20-min time trial.

evidence.quote: Functional threshold power is defined as the highest power output a cyclist can maintain in a quasi-steady state for approximately 60 min
could theoretically be determined as 95% of the mean power output in a 20-min time trial

claims.text: MLSS is found from about 4–5 constant 30-min rides on separate days: the highest one at which blood lactate rises no more than 1 mmol·L⁻¹ between minutes 10 and 30.

evidence.quote: The MLSS is conventionally derived from a series (typically 4–5) of 30 min continuous exercise bouts, completed on separate days
the MLSS is defined as the highest speed or power output that does not result in a rise of blood [lactate] of greater than 1 mmol/L between 10 and 30 min

steps.title: Is FTP really one-hour power?
steps.text:
In 23 trained men, 95% of 20-min power (FTP20) matched 60-min power on average: the mean gap was only 1–5 W. But the [limits of agreement](g:limits-of-agreement) were wide, roughly ±40–60 W, so for one rider the two could differ a lot. Riding to exhaustion at FTP20 lasted 51 ± 16 min, not 60 [[c:ftp20-60]].

Time at FTP also depends on level: a median of 35 min in recreational riders, rising to 51 min in professionals [[c:ftp-tte]].

A review of 15 studies, mostly of trained men, found FTP20 repeatable, but not interchangeable with other markers [[c:ftp-scoping]]. So FTP is a fair group estimate, yet for many riders not a power they can hold for an hour.

claims.text: FTP20 and 60-min power agreed on average (bias 1–5 W) but with wide limits of agreement, and time to exhaustion at FTP20 was about 51 min.

evidence.quote: Bland-Altman plots between FTP20, FTP60 and IAT showed small bias (-1 to -5 W), but large limits of agreement ([-40 to 32 W] to [-62 to 60 W]).
Time to exhaustion at FTP20 was 50.9±15.7 min.

claims.text: Median time to exhaustion at FTP rose from 35 min in recreational cyclists to 51 min in professionals.

evidence.quote: The median (interquartile range) time to exhaustion at the functional threshold power was 35 (31-38) minutes for recreationally trained cyclists, 42 (38-51) for trained ones, 47 (41-56) for well-trained ones and 51 (44-59) for professional level cyclists.

claims.text: FTP20 is reliable, but it shows wide limits of agreement with other markers, so they cannot be swapped.

evidence.quote: The FTP20 test was reported as a reliable test.
Studies investigating the relationship of FTP20 with other physiological markers and power-related concepts reported large limits of agreement suggesting parameters cannot be used interchangeably.
The majority of studies involved trained male cyclists.

steps.title: FTP and CP: close, not the same
steps.text:
In 17 trained cyclists and triathletes, CP was 7 W higher than FTP on average, with limits of agreement from −19 to +33 W: too wide to swap one for the other [[c:cp-ftp-agree]].

The physiology points the same way. In 13 cyclists, time to exhaustion was about 34 min at FTP and 22 min at FTP + 15 W, with end lactate of 6.7 against 9.2 mmol·L⁻¹. The authors concluded that FTP should not be read as the heavy–severe boundary [[c:ftp-not-mmss]].

The two numbers correlated almost perfectly (r = 0.97) [[c:cp-ftp-r]], yet still disagreed for single riders. A tight [correlation](g:correlation) says riders rank the same; it doesn't say their watts match.

claims.text: CP was on average 7 W above FTP, with limits of agreement of −19 to +33 W, so they should not be used interchangeably.

evidence.quote: The mean bias between CP and FTP was 7 ± 13 W and LoA were -19 to 33 W.
With relatively large ranges for LoA between variables, these values generally should not be used interchangeably.

claims.text: Time to task failure was about 34 min at FTP and 22 min at FTP + 15 W; FTP should not be taken as the heavy–severe boundary.

evidence.quote: The time to task failure at FTP and FTP +15W were 33.7 ± 7.6 and 22.0 ± 5.7 minutes
the end test blood lactate corresponding to FTP and FTP +15W was significantly different (6.7 ± 2.1 mM vs 9.2 ± 2.9 mM
suggests that FTP should not be considered a threshold marker between heavy and severe intensity.

claims.text: CP and FTP were strongly correlated (r = 0.969) despite the wide limits of agreement.

evidence.quote: Even though strong correlations exist between CP and FTP ( r  = 0.969;  P  < 0.001)

steps.title: CP or MLSS: which marks the steady-state limit?
steps.text:
MLSS usually comes out lower than CP: a [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 9 studies (104 people) found it about 11% below [[c:mlss-below-cp]]. Two readings:

- **CP is too high.** People hold CP for only 20–30 min, which hardly looks steady [[c:cp-unsteady]].
- **MLSS is too low.** MLSS rides go up in steps, and the answer is the last step that passed, so it sits below the true limit: with 30 W steps, about 15 W too low on average [[c:mlss-steps]].

With strict methods for both, one group found the gap shrank to a few watts [[c:few-watts]]. The debate is live; for training, what matters most is using one anchor consistently.

claims.text: MLSS was on average about 11% below CP in a meta-analysis.

evidence.quote: Despite the significant correlations between CP and VT1, MLSS and RCP these variables and VT2 under- (VT1, 30%; MLSS, 11%) or over-estimated (RCP, 6%; VT2, 21%) CP.
This resulted in 104 participants.

claims.text: Critics argue CP is too high to be a true steady state, since it can be held only for about 20–30 min.

evidence.quote: Much more than a critical mass of the extensive accumulated evidence, however, has persistently shown the determined intensity of critical power and its variants as being too high to maintain for extended periods.
exercise at CP being sustainable for no more than approximately 20-30 min

claims.text: Because MLSS is tested in steps, it underestimates the true limit: by about 15 W on average with 30 W steps.

evidence.quote: On average, with differences of 1 km/h or 30 W between discrete tests, the MLSS will be underestimated by 0.5 km/h for running or 15 W for cycling, respectively.
as presently defined, MLSS naturally underestimates the actual maximal metabolic steady state

claims.text: With strict determination criteria, CP and MLSS may differ by only a few watts.

evidence.quote: we demonstrate that differences between critical power and the maximal lactate steady state may be reconciled to only a few Watts when applying appropriate and strict determination criteria

debate.question: Does CP or MLSS mark the maximal metabolic steady state?

sides.position: CP is the real boundary: above it nothing settles, and MLSS sits below it partly because of how it is tested.
CP is set too high to be a steady state: it can be held only briefly, so MLSS is the better marker.
With strict methods for both, the two agree within a few watts and either can be used.

points: FTP is a performance number (about an hour, usually 0.95 × 20-min power); CP is the asymptote of the power–duration curve; MLSS is the top power with steady lactate.
FTP20 matches hour power on average, but limits of agreement are wide and many riders last only 35–55 min at it.
CP and FTP correlate closely yet differ by up to about 30 W in single riders: correlation is not agreement.
MLSS usually sits about 11% below CP. Whether CP is too high or MLSS too low is debated; strict methods shrink the gap.
For training, pick one anchor, measure it the same way each time and know what it means.

variants.stem: Which marker is defined by blood lactate across 30-min rides at constant power?

options.text: MLSS
options.why: Right: MLSS is the highest power where lactate rises no more than 1 mmol·L⁻¹ from minute 10 to 30.

options.text: FTP
options.why: FTP is a power-only field test: 95% of a 20-min effort, no blood needed.

options.text: CP
options.why: CP comes from power and time to exhaustion in 2–15 min efforts, no lactate needed.

options.text: VO2max
options.why: VO2max is the top of oxygen uptake, measured with a gas analyser in a ramp test.

variants.stem: A rider averages 300 W in a 20-min all-out test. What FTP does the usual rule give?

options.why: Right: FTP = 0.95 × 20-min mean power.
That is the 20-min power itself; FTP takes 5% off, since an hour is longer than 20 min.
This adds 5% instead of taking it off.
This takes off 10%; the usual rule is 5%.

variants.stem: A triathlete averages 260 W in a 20-min test. What FTP does the usual rule give?

options.why: Right: FTP = 0.95 × 20-min mean power.
That is the 20-min power itself; FTP takes 5% off, since an hour is longer than 20 min.
This adds 5% instead of taking it off.
This takes off 10%; the usual rule is 5%.

variants.stem: A rider averages 320 W in a 20-min test. What FTP does the usual rule give?

options.why: Right: FTP = 0.95 × 20-min mean power.
That is the 20-min power itself; FTP takes 5% off, since an hour is longer than 20 min.
This adds 5% instead of taking it off.
This takes off 10%; the usual rule is 5%.

variants.stem: A recreational rider's FTP from a 20-min test is 285 W. She tries to hold 285 W for an hour and cracks at 40 min. Best interpretation?

options.text: Common: many riders last well under an hour at FTP
options.why: Right: median time at FTP was 35 min in recreational riders, and the mean was about 51 min even in trained men.

options.text: Her 20-min test must have been done wrong
options.why: A correct test still gives an FTP that many riders can't hold for 60 min.

options.text: Poor fuelling is the only possible explanation
options.why: Fuel rarely limits a 40-min effort; the FTP rule itself overestimates hour power for many.

options.text: Her FTP must be above her VO2max
options.why: FTP sits well below VO2max power; the issue is the 95% rule, not VO2max.

variants.stem: FTP20 and 60-min power differed by only 1–5 W on average, but the limits of agreement ran from about −60 to +60 W. What does this mean for one rider?

options.text: The averages match, but her two numbers could be tens of watts apart
options.why: Right: limits of agreement describe single riders; wide limits mean one can't stand in for the other.

options.text: The two are the same for everyone, give or take 5 W
options.why: The 1–5 W is the group average; single riders scattered far more widely.

options.text: FTP20 always reads 5 W too high
options.why: The bias is an average, not a fixed offset for each rider.

options.text: The two must be unrelated
options.why: They correlated well; agreement and correlation are different questions.

variants.stem: Which statement describes CP, and not FTP or MLSS?

options.text: The level the power–duration curve flattens towards, from several 2–15 min efforts
options.why: Right: CP is the asymptote of the hyperbola, fitted from several severe efforts.

options.text: The power a rider is meant to hold for about an hour
options.why: That is the definition of FTP.

options.text: 95% of the mean power of one 20-min all-out test
options.why: That is how FTP is usually estimated.

options.text: The top power at which lactate rises ≤1 mmol·L⁻¹ over 20 min
options.why: That is how MLSS is defined.

variants.stem: A coach reads that CP and FTP correlate at r = 0.97 and decides he can set any rider's zones from either. What is wrong with his reasoning?

options.text: Correlation shows riders rank alike, not that their watts agree
options.why: Right: despite r = 0.97, single riders' CP and FTP differed by up to about 33 W.

options.text: Nothing: r = 0.97 means the two are the same number
options.why: A high r allows a large, varying gap between two measures; it is not agreement.

options.text: The correlation is too weak to mean anything
options.why: 0.97 is a very strong correlation; the problem is what it measures.

options.text: Correlations can't be computed between two powers
options.why: They can; it just answers a different question from agreement.

variants.stem: MLSS rides are done at 240, 270 and 300 W. Lactate passes the test at 270 W but rises 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹ from minute 10 to 30 at 300 W. What can you say about the true MLSS?

options.text: It lies somewhere from 270 W up to just under 300 W
options.why: Right: 270 W passed and 300 W failed, so the true limit lies between; calling it 270 W is a floor.

options.text: It is exactly 270 W
options.why: 270 W is just the highest step tested that passed; the real limit can be higher.

options.text: It is exactly 285 W, halfway between
options.why: Halfway is a guess; the test only brackets the limit.

options.text: It is above 300 W
options.why: 300 W failed the lactate test, so the limit is below it.

variants.stem: A forum post says: "CP overestimates the steady state, so MLSS is the gold standard." Best evaluation?

options.text: Disputed: each side has evidence, and strict methods narrow the gap
options.why: Right: the step test biases MLSS low, yet CP lasts only 20–30 min; with strict methods the two come close.

options.text: Settled: the meta-analysis proved MLSS is the true limit
options.why: The meta-analysis showed MLSS is lower, not which one is the true limit.

options.text: Settled the other way: CP comes from maths, so it can't be wrong
options.why: CP is fitted to noisy efforts, and its meaning is exactly what is debated.

options.text: Pointless: CP and MLSS are just two names for one number
options.why: They are found differently and usually differ, which is why the debate exists.

variants.stem: The study showing FTP20 lasts about 51 min tested 23 trained men. A recreational woman wants to use it to plan her hour. What most limits the finding for her?

options.text: Only trained men were tested, and less-trained riders last even less at FTP
options.why: Right: the sample doesn't match her, and another study found time at FTP shorter in recreational riders.

options.text: 23 people is too many for a lab study
options.why: A bigger sample is a strength, not a limit; 23 is if anything small.

options.text: Limits of agreement are not a valid way to compare tests
options.why: They are the standard way to judge whether two measures can be swapped.

options.text: Power meters can't measure 20-min power
options.why: Power meters measure it well; the issue is who was studied.
